questions.feedback: In a cadenza, the soloist plays a free, showy passage while the orchestra is silent.

evidence.supportingText: A prominent solo passage in a concerto or similar work, designed to display the performer's expressive and technical skill. It may be unaccompanied or lightly accompanied and often appears near the end of a movement. Cadenzas were historically improvised by performers, although many are now written into the score. In a concerto, listen for the soloist playing alone or with little accompaniment, often finishing with a trill before the orchestra returns.
evidence.verification: Checked against local extended definition and corresponding short definition/listening cues; no recording audition or independent specialist certification.

questions.feedback: Impressionist: This style suggests moods and images through tone colour, blurred harmonies and scales such as the whole-tone scale. Debussy is a well-known composer of it.

evidence.supportingText: A late-19th- and early-20th-century style that emphasises atmosphere, suggestion and tone colour rather than strongly directed tonal drama. questions.feedback: Augmentation makes a melody’s notes longer, often twice as long, while the beat stays the same.

evidence.supportingText: A theme, melody or rhythm is repeated with every note value lengthened in the same proportion. The material therefore takes longer while retaining its pitch and rhythmic relationships. The underlying pulse remains unchanged even though the transformed idea sounds slower. questions.feedback: Diminution makes a melody’s notes shorter, often half as long, while the beat stays the same.

evidence.supportingText: A theme, melody or rhythm is repeated with every note value shortened in the same proportion. The material therefore moves more quickly while retaining its essential pattern. The underlying pulse remains unchanged even though the transformed idea sounds faster. A common example halves the note values, so crotchets become quavers while the beat keeps the same speed.

questions.feedback: Harmonics: Lightly touching a string to make a high, clear, ringing note.

questions.feedback: Tremolando rapidly repeats notes to create a trembling sound.

evidence.supportingText: A rapid repetition or alternation that creates a trembling or wavering sound. On bowed strings it is commonly made by rapid bow strokes on one note; on other instruments it may involve repeating one note or alternating quickly between two notes. When two pitches alternate, they are normally at least a third apart, unlike the neighbouring notes of a trill.

questions.feedback: Serial: This compositional method organises music using a fixed ordering of pitches, often all twelve semitones before any is repeated.

evidence.supportingText: Music organised by a predetermined series rather than traditional functional tonality. Arnold Schoenberg developed twelve-tone serialism in the early 20th century.

questions.feedback: Appoggiatura: A leaning note that briefly clashes, then steps onto a more settled note.

evidence.supportingText: An expressive non-chord note that takes a significant part of the following main note's value. It normally creates accented dissonance, is approached by leap and resolves by step into a chord note. In a common traditional interpretation, it takes half the following note's value, or two-thirds when that note is dotted.

questions.feedback: Fugue: In this contrapuntal form, parts enter in turn with a subject and answer, followed by further entries and contrasting episodes.

evidence.supportingText: A contrapuntal work built from a subject introduced successively by several independent voices. In the exposition, the first voice states the subject, the next normally gives an answer at the dominant while the first continues with a countersubject, and further voices enter in turn. Later subject entries alternate with episodes and may use devices such as sequence, inversion or stretto.

evidence.supportingText: A vocal technique between speech and singing. The performer follows indicated pitch contours or starting pitches but releases them into speech-like inflection, producing a dramatic, heightened form of spoken delivery. The technique is strongly associated with early-20th-century works by Schoenberg and Berg.

media.recording: Vincenzo Bellini - Ah Non Giunge - Coloratura
media.libraryPath: 04. Higher/05. Timbre/Coloratura/01. Vincenzo Bellini - Ah Non Giunge - Coloratura.m4a

evidence.supportingText: Highly agile, ornamented vocal writing involving rapid scales, arpeggios, leaps, trills and other decorations. It is especially associated with high soprano roles and displays the singer's range and technical control. The style became prominent in Baroque vocal music and may include both written and improvised ornamentation. Many of the rapid notes are sung on a single syllable, creating an extended melismatic run.

evidence.supportingText: Highly agile, ornamented vocal writing involving rapid scales, arpeggios, leaps, trills and other decorations. It is especially associated with high soprano roles and displays the singer's range and technical control. The style became prominent in Baroque vocal music and may include both written and improvised ornamentation. Many of the rapid notes are sung on a single syllable, creating an extended melismatic run.

Many of the rapid notes are sung on a single syllable, creating an extended melismatic run.

media.libraryPath: 05. Advanced Higher/01. Styles/Madrigal/03. Cipriano de Rore - Madrigali À 5 Voci, Libro 5 - No. 2, Da Le Belle Contrade - Madrigal.m4a

evidence.supportingText: A secular Renaissance vocal work, usually for several unaccompanied voices. It is commonly polyphonic and through-composed, with changes of texture, rhythm and harmony used to reflect the meaning of the words. In the English madrigal tradition, English texts, word painting and a cappella performance are common features. Imitation is common: one voice begins a melodic idea and another copies it shortly afterwards.
